description_full: BJ's Restaurants, Inc. operates full-service restaurants in the United States. Its restaurants offer pizzas, crafts and other beers, appetizers, entrées, wings, pastas, sandwiches, specialty salads, and Pizookie desserts. The company was formerly known as Chicago Pizza & Brewery, Inc. and changed its name to BJ's Restaurants, Inc. in August 2004. BJ's Restaurants, Inc. was founded in 1978 and is based in Huntington Beach, California.
ceo_bio: Mr. Lyle D. Tick | CEO, President & Director | Age 49 | Compensation: $1.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 22K people. Revenue per employee of $61K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 7%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $1K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $388 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 25× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: BJ's Restaurants, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.2B market cap on $1.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +20% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at -1% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $25M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 6.08× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.0×.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.9% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 1% operating margin trails the Consumer Cyclical median (8%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.13x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-32.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 77% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 16% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 1.17, it moves roughly with the market.
About $27.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 85% in the 2020 crash, 43% in the 2022 bear market and 61% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $32.65 (margin of safety -71%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 12%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $19.77 to $54.14 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 29.8 vs 19.3 and P/FCF 48.2 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 380% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.1% (below the risk-free rate).
The 7 covering analysts target $74.71 on average, 34% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 1% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.31).
It converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-8.1% of assets).
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($26.1M of cash against $66.5M of debt), with interest covered 3.0x.
The current ratio of 0.41 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
It runs on negative working capital (-31 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 20.4% over 3 years, 4.0% over 5 years and 5.8% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
Free cash flow has compounded -19.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 5.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 5, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 25.4% on average.
Analysts expect 14.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 5 sales over the past year, net $4.5M sold.
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 2.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 12.2% of the float, 5.0 days to cover.
people: With about 22,230 employees, each generates about $61K of revenue, 0.2x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 6.7% a year.
That works out to $1K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.6M (25x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
